description:
En el polo sur de la Luna, unos cientos de metros de diferencia pueden definir si un módulo de aterrizaje tiene energía y comunicación con la Tierra, o no. T-Minus busca hacer visible esa diferencia.

Proyecto individual desde Buenos Aires.
summary:
T-Minus is a mission clock for the Moon's south pole.

Pick a landing site and a date, and it counts down to sunset and Earthset over the real lunar terrain, which tells you how long a lander will have power (Sun) and direct-to-Earth communication (Earth).

At the pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth bobs up and down behind mountains, so a few hundred meters can change everything: 500 m from Malapert's summit, Earth stays in view 100% of the time but sunlight drops by more than 11 points.

T-Minus turns NASA's ephemeris and LOLA topography into clear countdowns and maps. Mission planners can compare sites and replan instantly when a launch slips, and teachers and the public can see why lunar landing-site selection is so hard.

It also checks the "second horizon": whether a ground station such as ESA's Malargüe antenna in Argentina, or NASA's Deep Space Network, can see the Moon at that moment.
details:
Detailed Project Description

What it does

  • Countdown clocks per site: time until sunset and until Earthset (or until the next sunrise/Earthrise), measured against the real terrain horizon, with green/amber/red margins.
  • Date and schedule slip: a date picker plus a ±60-day "launch slipped" slider. Everything recalculates instantly, and playback shows how conditions evolve.
  • Two-horizon link check: direct-to-Earth contact needs Earth above the lunar terrain and the Moon above a ground station's horizon (10° mask). T-Minus checks ESA Malargüe (Argentina) and NASA DSN Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra.
  • Visualizations: a 360° horizon panorama with Sun and Earth tracks, a timeline of days with light, signal or both, side-by-side comparison of up to 3 sites, and window metrics (sunlit %, Earth-visible %, longest darkness, longest communication gap).
  • Explore: a 10 × 10 km map around each polar site (441 points, 500 m apart) with Sun / Earth / both heatmaps. Click any point to compute its countdowns in the browser. Custom coordinates are also supported.
  • Curated sites: Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Shackleton rim, Peak near Shackleton, de Gerlache rim, Malapert massif, Mons Mouton (IM-2 site), Nobile Rim 1, plus Chandrayaan-3 and Apollo 11/17 for comparison.
  • Educator mode: plain-language explanations.

How it works

  1. Sun and Earth positions are computed with NAIF SPICE kernels (DE421, lunar body-fixed frame) via Skyfield, at 10-minute steps for Nov 2026 – Dec 2028, from an observer on a 2 m mast. No atmospheric refraction. Libration is included through the lunar orientation model.
  2. For each site, the terrain horizon is ray-traced across 720 azimuths over NASA LOLA topography: the 5 m/pixel site DEMs (NASA PGDA) near the site, and the 120 m polar DEM out to 150 km.
  3. Sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset events, visibility fractions and station coverage are precomputed offline and served as static data. The web app has no runtime API calls.

Validation

  • Sun/Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.04 arcsec (1050 comparisons).
  • Run on the same 120 m terrain, our method reproduces NASA PGDA's published illumination and Earth-visibility maps with a median difference of about 1 percentage point.
  • At Connecting Ridge we get 89.9% sunlight at 2 m and 95.7% at 10 m, consistent with Gläser et al. (2014): 92.27% and 95.65%.

Full tables are in the Validation tab and in docs/VALIDATION.md.

Benefits

  • Fast, accessible what-if analysis for landing sites and dates.
  • Shows clearly why small changes in location or date matter.
  • Free, open source, and runs in any browser.

Tools

  • Pipeline: Python (Skyfield, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj).
  • Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite, Canvas; hosted on Vercel.
  • Video visualizations: three.js.
  • Video production: ffmpeg, CapCut.
